Agents are programs that let a language model decide what to do next. The model reads the conversation, answers with text or asks for a tool, and the program runs the tool and sends the result back. This loop repeats until the model has a final answer. Most of the time is spent waiting for the model, but every step also costs some work on our side: building the request, reading the streamed answer piece by piece, parsing JSON, calling the tools and keeping the history. When one process serves many users at the same time, that work adds up, and it shows as higher latency, lower throughput and more memory.

A small and fast core keeps that overhead low, so the program spends its time on what matters: the model and the tools. Streaming makes the answer appear sooner, because each token is shown as soon as it arrives instead of after the whole answer is ready. It also means many small events, and handling each of them must be cheap.

Tools are just functions with a description and a schema of their arguments. The model chooses when to call them and with which arguments, and it can call several tools at once. Running them concurrently saves time when they wait on the network or the disk.

A good agent library keeps all of this simple: you write the prompt and the tools, and the library takes care of the loop, the streaming and the errors. Measuring it honestly means using the same fake model, the same prompts and the same tools for every library, running each one in its own process, and repeating the measurement enough times to trust the numbers. That is what this benchmark does, and the results show where the time and the memory go.

Keep in mind that a real model is much slower than this fake one, so in production the differences are smaller than they look here.
